> "Because you don't have to create different policies for different job functions, you create fewer policies."

### iam-abac-recommended-only-within-own-organization

**Claim.** The Security pillar recommends using ABAC for access control only when both the principals and the resources belong to your own organization, because an external party can use the same tag names and values.

**Write it as.** `only be used for access control when both the principals and resources are owned by your AWS Organization` · `External parties may use the same tag names and values as your organization`

**Scope.** ABAC with tags, principals and resources of your own organization.

> — [SEC03-BP02 Grant least privilege access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/security-pillar/sec_permissions_least_privileges.html)

### iam-abac-tag-match-allows-all-resources

**Scope.** attribute-based access control in IAM.

### iam-access-denied-message-names-policy-type

**Claim.** An access denied message for an explicit deny includes the phrase 'with an explicit deny in a <type> policy' and may give the policy ARN; for an implicit deny it says 'because no <type> policy allows the <action> action'. If several policy types deny a request, only one type is named.

**Write it as.** `with an explicit deny in a <type> policy` · `because no <type> policy allows the <action> action`

**Scope.** access denied error messages (services that support the format).

> "When a policy explicitly denies access because the policy contains a `Deny` statement, then AWS includes the phrase `with an explicit deny in a {{type}} policy` in the access denied error message."

> "When the policy implicitly denies access, then AWS includes the phrase `because no {{type}} policy allows the {{action}} action` in the access denied error message."
> — [Troubleshoot access denied error messages](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/troubleshoot_access-denied.html)

**Claim.** If a condition key named in a policy is not present in the request context, the condition is false (true for a negated operator such as StringNotLike); this logic applies to all condition operators except the ...IfExists operators and the Null check, which test whether the key is present. Adding IfExists to an operator makes a missing key evaluate as true; IfExists can be added to any operator except Null.

> "This logic applies to all condition operators except ...IfExists and Null check. These operators test whether the key is present (exists) in the request context."
> — [IAM JSON policy elements: Condition operators](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html)

> "You do this to say "If the condition key is present in the context of the request, process the key as specified in the policy. If the key is not present, evaluate the condition element as true.""
> — [IAM JSON policy elements: Condition operators](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html)

> "You can add `IfExists` to the end of any condition operator name except the `Null` condition—for example, `StringLikeIfExists`."

### iam-external-id-prevents-confused-deputy

**Claim.** The confused deputy problem is when an entity without permission coerces a more privileged entity to act for it; for third-party cross-account access the external ID is an sts:ExternalId condition in the role's trust policy, with a value generated and controlled by the third party and unique per customer. When a role's trust policy includes an external ID, anyone who wants to assume the role must be a principal in the role and must include the correct external ID.

**Write it as.** `an entity without permission coerces a more privileged entity to act for it` · `an sts:ExternalId condition in the role's trust policy` · `generated and controlled by the third party and unique per customer`

**Scope.** third-party cross-account role access.

> "The confused deputy problem is a security issue where an entity that doesn't have permission to perform an action can coerce a more-privileged entity to perform the action."
> — [The confused deputy problem](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html)

> "Example Corp can address the confused deputy problem by requiring that you include the `ExternalId` condition check in the role's trust policy. Example Corp generates a unique `ExternalId` value for each customer and uses that value in its request to assume the role. The `ExternalId` value must be unique among Example Corp's customers and controlled by Example Corp, not its customers."
> — [The confused deputy problem](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html)

> "This `Condition` tests the `ExternalId` context key to ensure that it matches the unique customer ID from Example Corp."
> — [Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html)

> "In other words, when a role policy includes an external ID, anyone who wants to assume the role must be a principal in the role and must include the correct external ID."
> — [Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html)

> "The primary function of the external ID is to address and prevent The confused deputy problem."
> — [Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

**Write it as.** `including anonymous users (public access)` · `principals in other accounts also need identity-based permissions`

**Scope.** Principal element of a resource-based policy; Allow effect.

For IAM users and role principals within your account, no other permissions are required. For principals in other accounts, they must also have identity-based permissions in their account that allow them to access your resource."

**Write it as.** `does not grant a user permission to do anything` · `SCPs act as filters that specify the maximum permissions`

**Scope.** SCP Allow statements; maximum.

> "Even though this statement uses the same `Allow` value keyword as an IAM permission policy, in an SCP it doesn't actually grant a user permission to do anything. Instead, SCPs act as filters that specify the maximum permissions for the accounts in an organization, organizational unit (OU), or account."
> — [SCP syntax](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_syntax.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-11.

> "SCPs don't affect users or roles in the management account. They affect only the member accounts in your organization."

**Scope.** IAM users with long-term access keys; scenarios in which you need IAM users with programmatic access.

> "There are specific use cases that require long-term credentials with IAM users in AWS. Some of the use cases include the following:"
> — [Security best practices in IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

> "In some situations, you can't use IAM roles to provide temporary credentials, such as for WordPress plugins. In these situations, use IAM user long-term access keys for that workload to authenticate to AWS."
> — [Security best practices in IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

> "Third-party AWS clients – If you are using tools that don’t support access with IAM Identity Center, such as third-party AWS clients or vendors that are not hosted on AWS, use IAM user long-term access keys."
> — [Security best practices in IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

### iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not

**Claim.** An IAM user has long-term credentials (a password and access keys); a role has no standard long-term credentials and gives temporary security credentials for each role session. AWS recommends relying on temporary credentials instead of creating IAM users where possible.

**Write it as.** `does not have standard long-term credentials, such as a password or access keys` · `IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys` · `identities with long-term credentials`

**Scope.** IAM users and IAM roles.

> "Also, a role does not have standard long-term credentials, such as a password or access keys, associated with it. Instead, when you assume a role, it provides you with temporary security credentials for your role session. Unlike IAM roles, IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys. Where possible, best practices recommend relying on temporary credentials instead of creating IAM users who have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys."
> — [Root user best practices for your AWS account](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)

> "IAM users are identities with long-term credentials."
> — [AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) FAQs](https://aws.amazon.com/iam/faqs/)

**Checked.** 2026-10-11.

### iam-vpc-endpoint-policy-extra-boundary

**Claim.** A VPC endpoint policy is attached to a VPC endpoint to control which principals can use it and which resources can be reached through it; it acts as an additional access boundary for traffic through the endpoint.

**Write it as.** `an additional access boundary scoped to traffic that traverses the endpoint`

> "VPC endpoint policies act as an additional access boundary scoped to traffic that traverses the endpoint."
> — [Policies and permissions in AWS Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.
